content: Fingertip entrapment injuries in children typically involve damage to the soft tissue of the fingertip (pulp and nail) and often include fractures of the underlying bone. These injuries are most commonly caused by crushing mechanisms. Treatment options are generally divided into two categories: conservative management, which involves cleaning the wound and applying a dressing, and surgical intervention, which includes repairing lacerations and stabilizing fractures. However, there is currently no consensus on the most effective treatment approach for these injuries. The objective of this study was to evaluate the benefits and risks of both surgical and conservative treatments for fingertip entrapment injuries in children. Specifically, the study aimed to compare different conservative methods, surgical versus conservative approaches, various surgical techniques, and post-treatment management strategies following either surgical or conservative care. To gather evidence, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Bone, Joint and Muscle Trauma Group Specialised Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the World Health Organization Clinical Trials Registry Platform. The search included studies published up to April 30, 2013, without restrictions on language or publication status. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that compared different interventions for treating fingertip entrapment injuries in children. The primary outcomes of interest were fingertip function, nail growth, nail deformity, and adverse events such as infection. Two authors independently reviewed the studies for inclusion, assessed the risk of bias, and extracted data. Disagreements were resolved through discussion. Two RCTs involving a total of 191 children (180 of whom were included in the analyses) met the inclusion criteria. Both trials had significant methodological limitations, including a high risk of bias due to the lack of blinding of participants, personnel, and outcome assessors. Neither trial reported data on fingertip function, nail growth, or nail deformity. The quality of the evidence for the reported outcomes was rated as low using the GRADE approach, indicating that further research is likely to significantly impact confidence in the findings and potentially alter the results. One trial compared the use of a seven-day course of antibiotics versus no antibiotics following formal surgical repair of fingertip entrapment injuries. In this trial, one child in each group developed an infection by day seven (1/66 in the antibiotic group versus 1/69 in the no-antibiotic group; relative risk [RR] 1.05, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.07 to 16.37). Both children who developed infections had more severe injuries, specifically partial fingertip amputations. The second trial compared two types of dressings—silicone net and paraffin gauze—used after either surgical or conservative management of fingertip entrapment injuries. In this trial, two out of 20 children in the silicone group and one out of 25 in the paraffin group experienced wound infections (RR 2.50, 95% CI 0.24 to 25.63). Additionally, one child in the silicone group and two in the paraffin group developed skin necrosis (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.06 to 6.41). All complications resolved with conservative treatment. The mean healing times and the mean number of dressing changes were similar between the two groups (silicone: mean healing time 4.1 weeks, paraffin: mean healing time 4.0 weeks; mean difference [MD] 0.10 weeks, 95% CI -0.61 to 0.81; silicone: mean dressing changes 4.3, paraffin: mean dressing changes 4.2; MD 0.10, 95% CI -0.57 to 0.77). However, the silicone dressing was less likely to adhere to the wound and caused less distress to the child during the one-week dressing change. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence from RCTs to guide key treatment decisions for managing fingertip entrapment injuries in children. The low-quality evidence from one trial does not provide conclusive support for or against the prophylactic use of antibiotics after surgical repair in reducing infection risk. Notably, the two children who developed infections had more severe injuries. Similarly, the low-quality evidence from the second trial does not allow for definitive conclusions regarding the impact of silicone net versus paraffin gauze dressings on healing time or complications (such as infection or skin necrosis) at four weeks post-treatment. However, silicone dressings may offer the advantage of easier removal during the first week. Further high-quality RCTs are needed to address these gaps in evidence. Future studies should ideally compare surgical and conservative treatment methods and include long-term outcome assessments, such as fingertip function, nail growth, and nail deformity, for at least three months following treatment.
